strengths: The paper identifies a useful limitation of fixed agent-count curricula: increasing the number of agents can ease sparse-reward exploration, so progressing from fewer to more agents is not universally appropriate.

SPMARL combines self-paced curriculum optimization with an existing MAPPO critic signal in a simple, potentially practical way. The direct SPRL comparison provides a meaningful ablation of the proposed teacher objective.

Experiments cover three qualitatively different settings and distinguish target-task evaluation from training-task rewards. Results support the usefulness of adaptive agent-count curricula, with a clear early-learning advantage over SPRL on Simple-Spread. Figure 3 reports five seeds and 95% confidence intervals.
The teacher diagram, pseudocode, generated-curriculum plots, and provided code link help readers understand the approach and offer a basis for reuse.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as learning progress is insufficiently justified. Equation (8) measures prediction error: even with a fixed policy and an exact value function, squared return residuals retain conditional return variance. High loss can therefore reflect irreducible randomness or poor critic fitting without indicating useful policy improvement. No controlled analysis establishes that this score predicts subsequent improvement or alleviates credit-assignment difficulty. Likewise, correlated samples within trajectories do not automatically establish the claimed estimation-stability advantage.

The comparisons leave the contribution relative to prior work unresolved. Replacing DyMA-CL, EPC, and VACL with a linear schedule omits their other mechanisms. On Simple-Spread, the linear baseline follows the direction explicitly identified as unfavorable, without testing a tuned more-to-fewer alternative. Relevant value-error-based task prioritization, such as Prioritized Level Replay, and reward-improvement curricula also deserve discussion and comparison; SPRL alone does not represent these alternatives.

The claim of consistently faster convergence than SPRL exceeds the demonstrated evidence. The XOR curves in Figure 5 nearly coincide, while Figure 7 primarily shows an early SMACv2 advantage with similar later performance. Quantitative learning-speed estimates with uncertainty would clarify the improvement. Evaluation uses one target configuration per benchmark, provides no sensitivity analysis for the performance threshold or critic-loss estimation, and explicitly describes seed counts and interval definitions only for Figure 3.

The optimization requires clarification to be mathematically and algorithmically reproducible. With the stated Dirac target, Equation (6)'s KL divergence is infinite whenever the curriculum assigns probability to other contexts; the practical target approximation must be specified. Additionally, Section 4.1 describes freezing the distribution after performance falls below the threshold during the second stage, whereas Algorithm 1 appears to resume learning-progress maximization. These rules can generate different curricula.

Despite the code link, important experimental details are absent from the manuscript, including core training settings, initial context distributions and bounds across tasks, most performance-threshold values, and the evaluation protocol. The XOR experiment also needs an explanation of changing action spaces and agent identity under parameter sharing. These omissions limit informed reproduction and assessment of the gains. Smaller presentation problems include the inconsistent reference to eight target agents in the five-versus-five SMACv2 experiment and calling the random curriculum a random policy.
